utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Oric, good morning to you. Can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours and distinguished gentlemen. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. Good morning also to the Defence team. I'm here together with Ms. Patricia Sellers, co-counsel, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to the learned colleagues from the OTP. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and together with Mr. John Jones, I represent the Defence for Mr. Oric. We have with us here our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good morning to you and your team. Any preliminaries before we start? Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Just in short, Your Honour. Yesterday, the Trial Chamber requested for maps. We have them now available, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: So the usher can ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: To clarify further, Your Honour, this is the map related to the region in which the witness testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. I appreciate that, Mr. Wubben, and thank you, Ms. Sellers, as well, for passing on the message. Can we continue with the witness, or are there any other preliminaries? Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no preliminaries to raise, Your Honours. I can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What about the next witness? Will we be starting with the next witness today?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, as discussed yesterday, it had been confirmed by the Trial Chamber that there might be a possibility to start this afternoon. That's how I -- that's how I had been informed. But at the same time, the witness is still being proofed, in the proofing schedule, so we tried to do our best. This morning, Defence counsel informed me that this witness will take two hours, two and a half hours, so I don't know to what time that will bring us to finalise for this witness, and that we are able to bring the next witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I have understood you well, you yourself don't know if we will be hearing the -- we'll be starting with this witness today, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I learned some other information next to me. Will you please bear me a moment to go over it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the case manager had been informed this morning that -- and that's information from the senior legal officer, that the witness is not projected to be heard in court today. So the next witness will apparently not be available as projected by us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move, in the meantime, and we'll tackle this later, we'll see what the situation is, because you either need another two and a half hours for briefing -- I don't know. Anyway, we'll see -- come to it later, depending on how much time Madam Vidovic will engage us in the cross-examination. You can escort the witness in, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to proceed with your cross-examination, with your testimony, and we will be finishing today for sure. May I just remind you that yesterday, you made a solemn declaration to testify the truth, and that you are still bound by that solemn declaration today once you are continuing with your testimony. Madam Vidovic. Please, again, don't forget to allow an interval between question and answer. Yes. Cross-examined by Ms. Vidovic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Gligic.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To my yesterday's question as to whether you saw anything in relation to the destruction of the Muslim property, you said that there were cases of some extremists going over the line, but that was merely on an individual basis. But actually, this isn't right, is it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 8th of May, 1992, some 100 Muslim houses were burnt down in Skelani itself and Zabokvica, and 26 more houses in the nearby Vodivca [phoen]; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't. The number of houses you mentioned is something I don't agree with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw none of that, then; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Skelani at the time. And there were some isolated events that took place, but I did not witness them. There were such incidents, and the authorities in Skelani did sanction the perpetrators, if any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that on the 7th and 8th of May, 1992, 140 Muslim houses were burnt down in Dobrak?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dobrak is some 5 kilometres away from Skelani. At the time, there were less than 50 houses in Dobrak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that 70 Muslim houses had been burnt down in Trubari?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this. Trubari is some 7 to 8 kilometres away from Skelani.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I just want to clarify. The question of the Defence counsel was, "Did you hear that on the 7th and 8th of May, 140 Muslim houses were burnt down in Dobrak," and now the answer was, "At the time there were less than 50 houses in Dobrak." Now, does that mean that Dobrak didn't have more than 50 houses? It would, of course, not have been possible to burn down 140. Or does that mean that 50 houses have burnt down in Dobrak? What was your realisation, or what did you want to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that this piece of information that madam here conveyed about the number of houses burned down in Dobrak, that there weren't as many houses in Dobrak at all. This Muslim village of Dobrak numbered some 50 to 60 houses in total.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I asked of the witness whether he had heard that, on the 7th and 8th of May, 140 Muslim houses were burnt down. I don't know how it was translated, not whether the number was burnt down. But I will rephrase.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that all the Muslim houses were burnt down in Dobrak on the 7th and 8th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were not burnt down, or you did not hear of that?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The houses were not burnt down because refugees from all parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina came to Skelani. These were Serb refugees. Some of them used to live in Dobrak up until just a few years ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, please answer briefly to my questions. Did you hear that all the Muslim houses in Visosnik were burnt down?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say Visosnik, you have to specify the village, because there's a Serbian village at Visosnik, up above, and below Visosnik there's a Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was a very specific one. Did you hear that all the Muslim houses in Visosnik were burnt down?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what to answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why don't you know how to answer this question? Do you know whether they were burned down or not? Or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, when you say Visosnik, there's a church there and a Serb village, and below Visosnik there's several Muslim villages. And I don't know which village I should refer to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to concentrate exclusively on the village. You need to concentrate mostly on the Muslim and only on the Muslim houses in that village or in that area, in the area of Visosnik, because the question was not whether all the houses in Visosnik had been burned down but whether the -- all the Muslim houses, houses belonging to Muslim families in Visosnik, had been burned down. Did you hear of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that all the Muslim houses in Trubari had been burnt down?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All the Muslim houses in Bukovik?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Resagici? It's a suburb of Skelani.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several houses set on fire in Resagici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These were some 20 houses, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that two to three houses were set on fire. I don't know who they belonged to, or why they were set on fire. I only saw that they were.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I didn't hear the question, the previous one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Again, I mean, you're moving too fast. Please, I appeal to both of you to slow down a little bit. The interpreter did not hear your last question, and basically I think we ought to repeat the last series of questions. Did you hear that all the Muslim houses in Trubari had been burned down? And you have answered: "I have no knowledge of this." And then Madam Vidovic, correct me if I'm wrong, or fill in where I get stuck. And then you asked: "All the Muslim houses in Bukovik?" And that's a question whether you heard that all the Muslim houses in Bukovik had been burned down, and you said: "I don't know." "In Resagici? It's a suburb of Skelani." And then what I have here is that you answered that: "There were several houses set on fire in Resagici." And then did you ask that "These were some 20 houses, weren't they?" Was that your complete question, Madam Vidovic, or did you ask something else?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After that, I asked: Did you hear that houses were burnt down in Kadrici?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So you have two questions in one that you need to answer. Your first question was: "There were several houses set on fire in Resagici," and then you were asked: "These were some 20 houses, weren't they?" And we have here that you answered: "I don't know. I know that two or three houses were set on fire. I don't know who they belonged to or why they were set on fire. I only saw that they were." When you referred to these two or three houses, you were referring to the two or three houses in Resagici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And now your next question is: "Did you hear that houses were also burnt down in Kadrici?" Could you answer that question now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that all the Muslim houses in Hadzici were burnt down?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there is no such village in the area where I live. And I'm referring to the name of the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there or isn't there?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there is, Your Honour. There is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's stop here for a moment. Yes, Judge Eser, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I just have a question. Yesterday you gave us a map where certain villages were marked. Now, I've tried to follow your questioning, and some of the villages you mentioned are on this map, marked. But when you produced the last one, I cannot find. Now, are these additional villages now? And I think it would also be interesting to know the distance between Skelani and the villages you mentioned. So, for instance, the distance from Skelani to Resagici is rather narrow, whereas the distance to Trubari seems to be rather far away from here. So perhaps it would be helpful to indicate the distance between Skelani, where the defendant -- where the witness lived, and the villages that you're asking for. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm asking questions concerning villages that are in close proximity to Skelani, some several kilometres, up to 10 kilometres at most. As for the villages that you cannot locate on the map, well, these are very small villages, with only a few houses, and they are not plotted onto the map. And my reason for putting these questions to the witness is that the witness, yesterday, testified specifically to the incidents in Kragljevode and in Jezero, and these localities are far off from Skelani, at a much greater distance than the ones I'm asking about now. As for Trubari, they are -- Trubari is located above Jezero, and that's all in the Skelani area. Your Honours, may I continue with my questioning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, go ahead. I just want to make sure that the village that you mentioned and the witness says doesn't exist in his area, that we have it right on the transcript. Can you repeat the name of that village, please, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Hadzici, okay. So we have it right. You have never heard of Hadzici in your area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that 27 Muslim houses were burnt down in Sulice, or alternatively, did you hear that all the Muslim houses in Sulice were burnt down?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All the Muslim houses in Knezovi?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All the Muslim houses in Barakovici?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the houses in Barakovici were set on fire. I was passing along that route and I saw that there were some houses ablaze.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, I would suppose -- I think it would be much, much, much better, and much fairer for all of us if, when you refer questions to the witness with relation to the destruction of Muslim houses, you put them in a time slot, whether we are talking of 1992 or 1993, and if we're talking of 1992, which part of 1992. I mean, at least either pre-May or pre-June, I don't know, I mean it's up to you. But we can then assess the answer of the witness with much more accuracy.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe it was perfectly clear from the question that I asked at the outset. I'm talking about two days only here, the 7th and 8th of May, 1992. It's my submission that all these villages that I'm asking questions in relation to were burned down on those two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So you concentrate your answers in relation to only those two days, the 7th and 8th of May, 1992. Did you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Madam Vidovic, for helping us understand better.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that, at the time, on the 7th and 8th of May, 1992 - that is the time period that I'm referring to - all the Muslim houses in Zgunja were burned down?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Donja Peci?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Donja Peci is a village never the Drina, close to the road. And I had heard that several houses had been torched.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Gornja Peci?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Mala Daljegosta?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Velika Daljegosta?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Tursunovici?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're saying Rijeka, not Rijeke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're quite right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were several Muslim houses there. I think two or three of those were actually torched.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Suljagici?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Lijesce?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single house was torched in Lijesce. There are both Serb and Muslim houses there, and refugees lived there later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that over those days, the 57 Muslim houses in Lijesce were actually not burnt down.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 22 Muslim houses in Tihici, what about those?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it that when you say "no," you mean to tell us that you haven't heard, you don't know about these. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may add something. The village of Tihici that madam has just referred to, she said there were about 20 houses there that had been torched, and I said no for the simple reason that there are not that many houses in that village. There were two or three families living there. Therefore, there may have been four, five, ten houses in the village. It was no village, after all, it was a mere hamlet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But were those two, three houses belonging to Muslims torched down, burnt, or not? Or do you know whether they were burnt or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard about Mr. Ahmo Tihic's house being torched. I think he was commander of the Muslim army for a while. I heard that his house had been torched.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But this shows me that you need to be more precise in your answer. When you were asked by Madam Vidovic, "The 22 Muslim houses in Tihici, what about those" and you had this information, you couldn't just answer no, you had to explain. It was the case of explaining, not just answering now. It was the case of telling us, first of all, "There were not 22 houses in Tihici but less, and I have only Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. heard that there was perhaps one house belonging to a certain Ahmo Tihic that was burned down." That should have been your answer, not no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour. It's been 12 years, as you know. All the trauma may have caused me to get the answer wrong. But I'm telling you now: There weren't that many houses in that particular village. Ahmo's house, his family's house, was torched.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I now wish to show a video clip. The duration is about 12 minutes. There are subtitles; however, we have noticed errors of a purely grammatical nature in the English. The errors are not essential, but they are grammatical. We have put together our own transcript of this video clip, and if I could have the usher's assistance now to distribute the transcript to the parties. And after that, can the technical booth, please, switch the Defence video on. This video was taken by Mr. Mustafa Sacirovic while he was serving as president of the commission on gathering war facts in Srebrenica, and a member of the Bosnia and Herzegovina committee of gathering facts in relation to the war. I would like to use D89, a document, a Defence Exhibit that we have used before, which explains the official capacity of Mr. Sacirovic. We have had this video clip copied and we submitted a copy to the OTP yesterday. We have also produced a copy for the Chamber. May the video now be played, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: The Defence counsel has given us a copy, and we thank them for letting us see the video beforehand. I'm happy that Ms. Vidovic has clarified who the presenter, Mr. Sacirovic, is. We just want to add, in addition to noting a couple of grammatical errors in the transcript, there appears one time in the video where the transcript -- there was no transcript, although there was some dialogue going on. To inform Your Honours, we have listened to that and we have understood what dialogue was going on. So just to put on the record that we do understand that there have been problems with the transcribing. We'll reserve any other objections for afterwards, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, witness, play close attention to the video.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, you have now seen the video. Is it still your position that the Muslims from these villages, the villages that you pointed out on the map yesterday, left their homes of their own free will?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said this already, haven't I? You can't ask me this question. You can ask me about what I did at Skelani, whether this was the case or not. I simply have no idea. This footage could have been taken by anyone. You can see that this man is carrying an automatic rifle and shooting a video. I have no idea when or why he shot this video, to begin with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, can you just please simply answer my question. I'm putting it to you that this footage was taken in the exact locations referred to by the person taking the video. But my question was of an entirely different nature. I didn't ask you to comment on that. My question was: Is it still your submission that the Muslims left their homes of their own free will and went to the woods to hide there?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're saying that their families left for Serbia of their own free will, also?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I initially said that there were families who remained or went to Srebrenica. As many as 70 per cent of women and children in those villages went with the Red Cross to Serbia, to Bajina Basta. There must be more accurate information available. I read about this in the press. And I know how many people left from Macedonia and Croatia, from the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come back to that slightly later. Let me take a different approach now. Did you hear that in May 1992 people were being burned alive in their homes, in the Muslim villages around Skelani?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, might I just said that one of the previous questions that learned counsel asked might have been too general. She was talking about the Muslims, and I didn't know whether she was locating the Muslims, particularly, in this video, from the towns in this video, or was the witness referring to the Muslims from Skelani. I think that might have caused a bit of confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. In the light of what has just been pointed out by Madam Sellers, would you like to put your question again, please, Madam Vidovic? And, witness, have you understood the point made by Madam Sellers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Would you please be kind enough to put the question again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, is it your testimony that the Muslim men from the villages around Skelani left their homes of their own free will?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my position in relation to Skelani, or rather, what used to be Skelani municipality at the time: All the Muslims living in the territory of the former local commune and the future municipality were perfectly fine. There were people who were too scared to go to Serbia, but about 70 per cent of the people in Skelani - I'll give you the exact families who crossed eventually, if that's what it takes - people left for Macedonia and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will ask you the following question: Did you hear that in May 1992, in the Muslim villages mentioned in the video, that you pointed out on the map yesterday, people were burned alive in their own homes?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the Muslims from the Muslim villages referred to in the video, such as, for example, Trubari, Radovcici, Tokoljaci, burned alive by Serbs in their own homes?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are comments being made in the footage about attacks from Jezero, more specifically, shelling from Jezero. Yesterday, you repeatedly referred to Jezero. It is true, isn't it, that the artillery of the Skelani Battalion was positioned at Jezero?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know that the Independent Battalion held the line at Jezero. As for all the Muslim villages near Jezero, that means those Muslim villages were not full, they were empty. How else could those people at Jezero have been holding the line if they'd had Muslims behind their backs?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This doesn't really answer my question, does it? I asked you about artillery, artillery positioned at Jezero in August 1992 through to the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something that I'm not familiar with. I was not at Jezero. I was not a military conscript.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before I move on to my next question, can this video please be assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. The number, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the video clip gets the exhibit number D177.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And the transcript gets the exhibit number D177.1, and the English translation gets the number D177.1E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would like to put on the record that the transcript or the voices that we have heard and seen on the video do not necessarily go to the truth of their statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: They just go to the fact that they were said by those people. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to stress that in the least. The video shows what it shows, but it doesn't prove that people were burnt alive, for example, or that things happened when they are supposed to be happening, except what we see directly on the video, all right? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance, please, and place on the ELMO an excerpt from the report by the Helsinki Watch, War Crimes in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in August 1992. The first two pages are the cover page, and a page showing that this is an issue of a report dating from 1992. Could the pages 60 and 61 of the Helsinki Watch report be shown to the witness. They refer to Skelani, the municipality of Srebrenica. Just to inform the witness, Helsinki Watch is a non-governmental organisation for the protection of human rights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Refrain from explaining to the witness what Helsinki Watch, or who is behind this report. Just go to the part of the report that you're interested in and put the question to him, all right?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will quote to you two passages. The first one is on page 60, and I will quote it to you: "According to eyewitnesses interviewed by Helsinki Watch representatives, men in the village of Skelani were summarily executed after the village fell to Serbian forces on May 7th. Vahida, Tima, and Malida Salimovic were married to three brothers, Asim, age 42, Kemo, age 31, and Rizo, age 27, and had a total of seven children. According to each of the three women, Serbs in the area declared Skelani to be a Serbian village on May 1st. On the same day, the Serbs demanded that all Muslims relinquish any arms in their possession by 300 p.m. that afternoon or risk being attacked. The Muslims complied and relinquished any guns, mostly hunting rifles, in their possession." I will go right on to the second quotation from page 61, and I will ask questions of you in relation to this: "According to independent Serbian press reports, after the fall of Skelani, 550 Muslims, mostly women, children, and elderly persons, were expelled from the village and taken to the Serbian border. Once they crossed 50 metres of the bridge into Serbia, Serbian authorities refused to grant them entry. Rather, when the refugees got to the Serbian side, the authorities turned them back into Bosnia and told them to go home. When the refugees turned back over the bridge, they were met by members of Bosnia's Serbian armed forces. They told the refugees that Skelani was not a Serbian village, and that they had no claim to it. Negotiations lasted from 500 p.m. to 1000 p.m., and finally it was decided that some of the refugees would be taken to Macedonia via Serbia." My question to you, Mr. Gligic, is the following one: You know that there were expulsions and murders taking place in Skelani, don't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no such thing taking place in Skelani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Asim, Kemo, and Rizo Salimovic from the Skelani hamlet of Resagici?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the villages around Skelani, for all those people, the Skelani authorities had organised buses and people were transported. Not a single refugee went to Serbia and was turned back the same day. That's not true. Women and children that left, left for Macedonia and Croatia, and after the war, they were returning to Tuzla and then on to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my question was:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Did you know Asim, Kemo, and Rizo Salimovic from the Skelani hamlet of Resagici?"

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember if they were in Resagici at the time. I knew them, but I claim to you that people, women and children, whoever wanted to go to Serbia, went to the Red Cross and were then transported by buses elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, do you know what the fate was of the people who I mentioned to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I move on to my next question, could these reports from the Helsinki Watch be assigned a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This will be Defence Exhibit 178; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, yesterday, you took an oath to tell the truth only before this Tribunal. In your 2000 statement, you said, and yesterday in answering my question, you said that the murders in Skelani started on the 9th of May, 1992, on account of those two incidents, as a result of which there were some Serb victims. But that's far from the truth, is it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim to you, and it will be easy for you to verify the information, the first victims in the municipality of Srebrenica and in the area of Skelani are Danilo Petrovic and the Simic family. The information is well known throughout the world. We know who got killed and who killed them. I only know that this was the cause of a bloody war that ensued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, I'm putting it to you that you knew of the events described by the Helsinki Watch, and you knew about them because you were personally involved in the persecutions and massacres.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. Those who returned to Skelani, there's maybe 100 of them now, you can double-check with them, you can inquire after me and my background, and you will find out that I was always an honourable neighbour. And I am still a friend of theirs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, please answer my questions. I'm putting it to you that in May, that is, in April, May and June, you were not a driver of the ambulance, as you have claimed, but that your role in these events was a very significant one.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you're saying is not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were the person selecting people on the bridge across the Drina between Skelani and Serbia, the way that the Helsinki Watch described.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. I lived with those people and I helped those people. They did not place their trust in the Crisis Staff. And I personally went to the village of Salihovici and Skelani unarmed. And all those people crossed the bridge and are still alive to document this. The Musici family, who were my neighbours for 50 years, Salihovici, Hasanovici, and others, all these people live in Skelani today. There are about 100 families. And all these people can testify as to my character.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will ask you about very specific events and issues. On the 7th of May, you were the one who supervised the entire operation of screening, selecting people on the bridge. Please answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that bridge, on the 7th of May, 1992, among others, three Bosnian Muslims were arrested; a former police officer of the Srebrenica police station, Mr. Nedzad Pribicevac, the underaged Mehmed Begovic, and Alagic. You knew these people, and they knew you, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if they knew me. I did not see these people at the SUP. They didn't work there. I knew who worked at the SUP Skelani, and I'm referring to the police officers there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, you grew up together with Mr. Nedzad Pribicevic?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. You said he was a police officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked whether you knew him. Yes, he was a police officer. But my question was: Did you know Nedzad Pribicevic?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nedzad was not a police officer, and yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: When they were arrested, they asked that you come, and you were the person who decided their fate. You ordered two soldiers to take those people to the police station. In actual fact, two of them, Mr. Nedzad Pribicevic and Nusret Malagic, were taken to be shot.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. The Crisis Staff informed some people - I don't know who - to go to that village. I went to the village and talked to Sabrija Salihovic, the teacher there, and his wife and his family, and all the other Muslim who were there. Of course, these people were afraid. When I got there, I provided guarantees to these people. They could have shot me if I was to be blamed for anything. I was unarmed, but they had arms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I haven't finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've still not answered the part of the question in which you were asked whether, when Nedzad Pribicevic and Nusret Malagic, when these people were being arrested, they asked that you come. Let's take it bit by bit. When these persons that you have mentioned before, Nedzad Pribicevac, Andric Mehmed something, Alagic, is it true that you were asked to be present? Let's take it bit by bit. Please answer yes or no. Are you aware that these persons were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those persons were not arrested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you know whether two of them, in particular, Nedzad Pribicevic and Nusret Malagic, were transferred to the police station on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. All those Muslims --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just these two, please. Nedzad Pribicevic and Nusret Malagic, are you aware of their transfer to the police station on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you aware that at some point in time, these two persons, Nedzad Pribicevic and Nusret Malagic, were taken to be shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the sake of the transcript, these were Nedzad Ibisevic and Nusret Malagic, they were taken to be shot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So I, again, repeat all the questions to you, without the need of reading them again. But when I said Nedzad Pribicevic, I meant Nedzad Ibisevic, and when I said Nusret Malagic, indeed, I meant Nusret Malagic. Are you aware that these persons were arrested on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And they were taken to the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that they were then taken to be shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you aware that they were, indeed, shot, killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Are you aware -- do you know if Nedzad Ibisevic is still alive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the same question with regard to Nusret Malagic. Are you aware -- do you know if Nusret Malagic is still alive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that Nusret Malagic is alive. He has a nickname, Kuljo. He's a tall man, very tall, blonde. And I know that he's alive. He did show up in Skelani afterwards, but I don't know where he was coming from, whether it was Tuzla or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Earlier on, you also said that you disagreed with Madam Vidovic that Nedzad Ibisevic was a police officer. If he was not a police officer, do you know what he was, what was his occupation at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we are talking about one and the same man, this man worked in Serbia for the Crni Vrh company, dealing with wood processing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you grew up with this same person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just to clarify this matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is true, is it not, and you are very well aware of this, that Nusret Malagic was shot on that occasion, and Nedzad Ibisevic survived the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. firing squad. He was wounded but he survived.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Gligic, you knew Omer Mehic's family from Skelani. This man had his own butcher shop in Skelani before the war; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 13th of May, 1992, you, together with your brother, your twin brother, barged into the Mehic family's house under the pretext that you were searching for weapons.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You found an old lady there, Hava Mehic, and you took her to the police station. And you and your twin brother set her house on fire.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. The Mehic family had a house in Skelani and a shop. They have one to this day. And their mother had a separate house in Jovcici. So in total they had three houses. And this hamlet is some 3 or 4 kilometres from Skelani, in the direction of Dubrove [phoen], that is, 6 or 7 kilometres in the direction of Dubrove. Their mother brought weapons to the sons that they had in the family. And this particular lady, I escorted her from the bridge, because she arrived in Skelani to the SUP, and she surrendered the weapons. I don't know what she had, but she got a receipt against it. And this lady has a daughter, Nena, she has a daughter, and we are on friendly terms. And she went to her daughter's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that you and your twin brother did not, in fact, torch that house?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. I had been close with that family and on visiting terms for over 30 years. I saw them over two years ago in Sarajevo. They run a huge shop there. They are well off financially. And now they, again, have a shop in Skelani. I'm friends with Omer, with Nurija, with her sons, with the entire family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm putting it to you that you are not on friendly terms with those people. But I'll ask you a different question now.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can easily check that. I saw Mujo about a month ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You took part in the persecution, detention, and execution of people from the Muslim hamlet of Resagici. What's more, you were part of the group of people that executed Kemo Salihovic, a name found in the Helsinki Watch report.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were involved in the arrest and detention of civilians in the community house in Skelani, or community home in Skelani. It is true that you were seen there on a number of occasions, bringing Muslims in, were you not?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true that Muslims were being held in that hall. As to the people who were in that hall, I helped whoever I could and whoever I knew. The hall was full. But people were not being detained there to be mistreated but to make it possible for them to leave for Serbia. I remember a small child, his mother's name is Mihic. I brought a bottle of milk for the child. Now this woman is back in the village of Zabokvica, with her father and husband.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, there were many people who failed to survive the torture that was inflicted on them at the community home in Skelani; isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, at the time I had more Muslim friends than Serb friends, and this is something that I'm paying a price for, even today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you something else, though. There were many people who didn't make it, who didn't survive the torture at the community home where you were a frequent guest, were you not?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did go there. I helped people. Those people eventually left for Serbia. Now, as to whether anyone murdered anyone else or tortured anyone else, I don't know anything about that, because I didn't witness any such scenes. But please, if you can find a Muslim who will point his finger at me, saying that I did any of that, do so, if you can. I am here to tell the truth, and all I can tell you about that is that I went there to help those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 1st and 2nd of June, 1992, you were a member of a unit that killed 13 civilians in the village of Joseva. Among these civilians, there was a 13-month-old baby. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I now have a different set of questions. Maybe this would be a convenient time to have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll have a break of 25 minutes, a 25-minute break, starting from now. Thank you. I think -- one moment. I think I better wait for the witness to leave the courtroom first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I see Mr. Wubben ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to update you regarding the next witness. We will schedule that next witness for tomorrow, as we are still on the proofing actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's understandable. We have no problems with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am making very slow progress, unfortunately, and I think we will be needing a bit more time with this witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, in your testimony yesterday, and in your statement to the investigators, you dropped the name of Mr. Besim Mandzic. You said he was president of the Srebrenica municipality in the year 2000; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This gentleman was a chief in Srebrenica at that period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's about the name, Besim Mandzic. This person was never, in fact, president of the municipality. In order to clarify, the president was Nesib Mandzic.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I believe I know full well who he was. He was a neighbour of mine. He was the mayor or the municipality president in Srebrenica at the time. I'm saying after the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the same person who, on the 11th of July, 1992, was publicly intimidated -- 1995, was publicly intimidated by Ratko Mladic in the presence of DutchBat representatives?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if he was intimidated. I know that in Skelani, the distance between his house and mine is up to 200 metres. He has a brother and sister, and I don't know whether they live in Denmark or in Holland. But I do know that a person from Skelani was the president of the municipality at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm putting it to you that Nesib Mandzic was the president of the municipality. At any rate, in early April 1992, he left Skelani for Tuzla where he remained until July 1992. And there was no way you could have seen him wearing a uniform or carrying a rifle in late April 1992, as you described to the investigators.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. I know this person really well. I know he was a representative in Srebrenica, and I know he was in Skelani at the time. He was a highly-positioned SDA official for the Skelani area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I'll move on to something else now. You stated that Skelani had no military facilities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is still my position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In actual fact, a great number of paramilitary units from Serbia were stationed there right from the beginning of the war, and at least up until the summer of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your submission that Zeljko Raznjatovic's, Arkan's unit, paramilitary unit, was not stationed there?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, that's my submission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Captain Dragan's unit?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Petar Cubilo, Peki's unit?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that a red beret camp was stationed there. These red berets were from Serbia and led by Nikola Pupovac. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Red Berets existed and they did indeed have a camp. Whether they were red and whether they were from Bosnia, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just a moment. It only gives some information but not what you asked. The question referred specifically to a Red Beret camp being stationed there, and you say the Red Berets existed, everyone knows this and they did indeed have a camp. Where was this camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was not a camp in the proper sense of the word. They had a base. The distance between the SUP and their camp was about 1 kilometre. I know that there was a unit in Sekovici where they had their command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So when you say "the SUP," you mean the SUP in Skelani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. From the SUP building, 1 kilometre down the Drina, at the far end of Skelani, facing Resagici, they had a base or headquarters. I'm not sure what I should call it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Can I have the usher's assistance, please. I would like to show the witness a document. The document is a document of the headquarters of the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, administration for OB affairs, dated the 28th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you please look at the relevant page of the document, which is page 3, paragraphs 4 and 5. I will read to you what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just inform the Chamber that we only have the first page translated, so that we can show what the document is. This is a very extensive document, and I have tried to ask the CLSS to translate as many documents for us as possible, but on the other hand we were asked by OLAD to only request to have the relevant sections translated when dealing with extensive documents. Therefore, we only have a translation of a section which refers to Skelani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, on page 3, if you can look at paragraphs 4 and 5, which I will now quote to you: "In the area of the Serb municipality of Skelani, a camp of the so-called Red Berets was formed and led by Pupovac Nikola, one of Captain Dragan's students. According to unverified information, this group is preparing for overthrowing and a takeover of power in the Serb municipality of Skelani. Paramilitary formations, led at the outset by Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, and subsequently by Captain Dragan, and recently by a person named Peki, stole goods and material property in the value of between 30 and 40 million German marks. For instance, about 10 tonnes of silver, between 3 and 4 tonnes of zinc, pharmacy with medicines, and everything was transferred to Serbia." My question to you is: Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, was a highly popular figure among Serbs at the time, was he not? And the same applies to Captain Dragan. You must have known of their presence in Skelani?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew these gentlemen from the media, and I put it to you that they were not in Skelani.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honours. May we have an exhibit number assigned to this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This will be D179, Defence Exhibit D179.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Skelani had an Independent Battalion on account of the village's importance. Wasn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Skelani had an Independent Battalion whose duty was to defend the village of Skelani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that the front line of Skelani's defence was near Jezero. Is that still your submission?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moreover, you, in a statement given to the Prosecutor in July 2000, on page 3, paragraph 2 - it is the same in the English version - said, I quote: "However, in September 1992, the headquarters of one battalion of the army of Republika Srpska was stationed or set up in Skelani in order to monitor and coordinate the front line that is more than 54 kilometres long, stretching across the village and around it." That is a statement that you made to the Prosecutors of this Tribunal in the year 2000, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you give me the exact date when you said the army of Republika Srpska arrived?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I said in September. I can read the passage out to you, or if you want me to, I can show you your statement, Mr. Gligic, if you consider that to be necessary. I said: "However, in September 1992," in September 1992, "the command centre of a Bosnian Serb army battalion set itself up in Skelani in order to monitor and coordinate a front line that extended in and around Skelani over a 54-kilometre radius."

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said was that the Independent Battalion was set up at that time. I'm not sure how it was translated into English. When I spoke about the Independent Battalion, I gave the exact names of people who were officers in that battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are saying that the front line did not run through Skelani itself, which is different from what you stated to the investigators.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From the beginning of September, there was a TO unit which the citizens set up in order to protect them from the Muslim units. In September, it became the Independent Battalion. Those were people watching their own houses and standing guard, and they were now subordinated to the Independent Battalion. The Independent Battalion at that point in time was subordinated to the corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, can you please follow my question closely and provide answers to my questions only.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the battalion was stationed at Jezero. That was the line they held. And they formed a semicircle at Jezero, including the Serb villages and Skelani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. There's no need for you to go through that again, because we've heard that before. The Skelani Battalion was a well-equipped and well-manned unit, was it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had between 400 and 450 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was: Was this a well-equipped unit, in the military sense of the word?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever weapons they had were stationed at Jezero and not in Skelani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that, for two months, you worked with the military section of the Crisis Staff. You knew exactly, didn't you, where the TO of Skelani got their weapons and equipment from?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My job was not about that. I was not in a position to see any of the battalion's orders or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, Mr. Gligic, it's true, isn't it, that the Skelani Battalion got their weapons and equipment from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. From the beginning of September, the Skelani Battalion formed part of the Drina Corps, and the headquarters, as everyone knows, was in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that, in late 1992 and up to April 1993, the Skelani Battalion did not receive any weapons from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lived in Skelani, and I should know. As for manpower, it was made up of men living in Bajina Basta, in Serbia, but who had been born in Skelani. They had left their homes previously; I don't know the reason. They should know. They came back to help their neighbours out, help their families, help their brothers to defend their homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, can you please pay close attention to what my questions are about. I asked you about weapons being received from Yugoslavia. Weapons.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance again, please, to place on the ELMO a document of the Drina Corps command, dated 4th of February, 1993, and sent to the Zvornik Brigade command. The OTP exhibit number or the ERN is 01225623.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you please have a look. Sir, I'll quote the document to you: "Based on your verbal request, you are to act in the following way: Send an authorised representative of your brigade to Skelani who will, in agreement with the command of the Skelani Independent Battalion, take the following amounts of ammunition from their storage." And then what we see here is 400 mortar shells and 100 bullets. "Upon the completion of the task, inform the corps command about the real quantities taken over." This is a document, Mr. Gligic, that the Drina Corps command sent to the Zvornik Brigade command. Is it true -- is it not true that there were other units in the same period that were receiving their weapons from the Skelani Battalion? Is this something that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the command, I'm not aware of anything in relation to that. What I saw in Skelani was that there were a great number of volunteers there from Bajina Basta. How many exactly, I really don't know, but they were around. And they came to defend their homes. And they went to Jezero. What exactly it was that they were doing, I really don't know. As for this document, I have nothing to do with this. This is about the corps, this is about the command, this is about generals, if you ask me. I was a simple driver. I have nothing to do with this, and I can hardly understand a document like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I told you yesterday when we started, please answer the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question. I notice that as we go along, you are answering everything except the question. And we can't go on like this. You'll be here forever.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before I move on to a different question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, this will be --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- this will be Defence Exhibit D180. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, you told us yesterday that you resided in the vicinity of the police station. Do you agree with me that the police staff in Skelani were numerous and well-armed?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance, please. I'd like to place on the ELMO a document by the Territorial Defence of the Serbian municipality of Skelani, number 28-21, dated 26 May 1992. This is a request for materiel and technical equipment, addressed to the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of the Serb people of BiH, for them in Sarajevo to be handed over the materiel and technical equipment for Skelani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, you have the document before you. Please look at the items contained in the request. They ask for 100 camouflage uniforms, 20 pieces of twill uniforms, and, among other things, under item 6, 100 automatic rifles, 10 sub-machine-guns. And the second last sentence goes as follows: "Please forward this fax to the federal SUP." My question to you, Mr. Gligic, is as follows: Even the police force in Skelani received their equipment from Yugoslavia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Gligic, that this request relates to a large quantity of equipment and weapons for such a small police station such as the one in Skelani?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By saying no, what did you exactly mean? That Skelani is not a small place or -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Skelani is a small village, and I know exactly how many police officers there were in Skelani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many police officers there were in Skelani?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police officers working for the SUP in Skelani, I can give you their names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us the number.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some ten police officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many reserve police officers were there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're jumping one on the other without the least hesitation. Please slow down and allow an interval of time between question and answer, because if we -- we can't go on like this. We can't go on like this. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many reserve police officers were there in Skelani?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were police officers for the reserve forces, but I don't know how many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a member of the Skelani Battalion, you were well-equipped, you were on a payroll; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was no salary, it was just a payment used by us for maintaining personal hygiene. And I received it sometimes from the SUP, sometimes from the battalion, and sometimes from the Crisis Staff. And not only I, but all those who were performing this work obligation, had duties to attend to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You didn't answer the other part of the question, which was whether you were well-equipped, as a member of the Skelani Battalion. Were you well-equipped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Part of the command was stationed in Skelani, and I was stationed there, and part of the battalion was positioned at Jezero.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know what has been -- how my question has been translated to you. My question was a very simple one: As a member of the Skelani Battalion, were you well-equipped? It's not where you were stationed but how you were equipped, whether you were well-equipped or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Are you referring to myself personally?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not. I had a pistol that I had from before the war, and I had a rifle that I was unable to use because I was in the car. But I did sign for a rifle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I just wanted, for the benefit of clarification, to make sure on what time we are talking. Now, in the last ten minutes, we had a document dealing with February 1993, we have been talking about April, May, 1992, and the Independent Battalion, I remember -- I think it was founded in September. Now, these are three different periods, and if questions are asked with regard with the amount of weapons and so on, I think it would be worthwhile to know which period you are talking about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards the weapons of the police, the document is dated the 26th of May, 1992, and the document describes the level of equipment that the police had in the course of 1992. As for the Skelani Battalion, we were referring to the period since its establishment in September 1992, and I mentioned April 1993. So that's the period in between.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: However --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, Your Honours, I will do my best to date my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Sorry. Just to make sure, only for clarification. The document of May 26th, 1992, speaks of a request, if there was a request. So does that necessarily mean that the weapons, they have been received in fact? So I think we should distinguish between requests and the factual state of weaponry at a certain time. Only to clarify the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did emphasise that it was a request for materiel and technical equipment, and I asked the witness whether it was unusual for such a small settlement as Skelani to be asking for such large quantities of weapons. That was the drift of my question. I was not inquiring after whether the weapons were delivered or not. But I'm sure that we will have a great many pieces of evidence to show through this witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Gligic, since the establishment of the Skelani Battalion, as you stated that it was in September 1992, so from that period onwards, your military superior officers received their salaries directly from Belgrade. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance, please. I would like to place a document on the ELMO, and I would like the witness to be shown the document. It's a document by the command of the Drina Corps, dated 23 November 1992. The document bears the number 01334728, and is entitled "Regulation of Settlements and Payments to Members of the Republika Srpska Army." The document was delivered to the Podrinje Light Brigade, Zvornik Light Brigade, Birca Infantry Brigade, Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, Skelani Independent Battalion, and the Romanija Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, Madam Vidovic, do you intend to tender the previous documents or document?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the previous document, which was referred to the witness in the previous questions, is being tendered and admitted and marked as Defence Exhibit D181.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, please take a look at the document. I will quote from it. "Commissioned officers and non-commissioned officers and the staff working on contract for the Republika Srpska army, who met on the 19th of May, 1992, in relation to these people, they will continue receiving payments deposited on their accounts. For the staff serving the army and their families in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, their payments, based on cheques, will be collected by authorised officials of the Republika Srpska army at the Belgrade postal savings account in the following manner..." And what follows is a detailed instruction as to how these personal incomes can be withdrawn. I will put a very specific question to you, Mr. Gligic: Do you know whether some members of the Skelani Battalion received their salaries from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned Rajko Kuljanin and Bosko Vukovic as the commanding officers. These were professional officers of the former JNA; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Bosko Vukovic, from the village of Toplice, worked in the military department in Srebrenica before the war. He was an official there. Where Vukovic worked, I'm not sure. I think he was a colonel or a lieutenant colonel. And Mr. Vukovic was a resident of my village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, if he wasn't a member of the former JNA, what was he a member of? Was he a member of the former JNA, of the army of Yugoslavia before the disintegration of ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Mr. Vukovic worked as a civilian for the military department in Srebrenica before the war, so he was a civilian. When the war broke out, he was a reserve -- a member of the reserve forces and had the rank of a captain, I believe. And that's how he became a member of the battalion. Mr. Kuljanin may have been a professional soldier. I don't know where he hailed from. I know his name was Rajko Kuljanin. I know that he came from the corps in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're not aware of the fact that Rajko Kuljanin came from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Can this document please be assigned an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This will be D182, Defence Exhibit D182.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In actual fact, in January 1993, in Skelani, there was a large army stationed there; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In January, in Skelani, that's to say, following the attack on the 16th, the army started arriving from the corps on the 18th, 19th and onwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
