utterances.text: I'm putting it to you, Mr. Gligic, that the army was stationed there throughout January 1993, and I mean in Skelani, and that these were not just men from Skelani and the surrounding villages who formed part of the Skelani Battalion.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it was on the 18th or 19th of January, 1993, that forces from the corps were deployed there, because the battalion was asking for help.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will ask you to answer some of my questions. It is true, is it not, that in the sector of Skelani, in the area of Skelani, there was the command headquarters of General Mile Mrksic in May 1993?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: In January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is true that the Guards Brigade of the Yugoslav army was stationed there, is it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Parachute Brigade of the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that the 72nd Airborne Assault Brigade from Pancevo was deployed there?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm putting it to you that parts of the Drina division were also stationed in Skelani.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I've understood your question. Where did they come from? The Drina division, where do they come from? I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you heard of the existence of the Drina division?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard of its existence, but it was not present in Skelani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's what you say. Very well. You must have been aware of the fact that some units belonging to the Uzice Corps had entered Skelani prior to the events in mid-January 1993 in Skelani?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say "the Uzice Corps," Bajina Basta comes under the Uzice Corps territory. And after the attack on the 16th of January, the residents of Bajina Basta, of their own will, for patriotic reasons, crossed the Drina River. But there must be records with the battalion in Bajina Basta there, because nobody was able to cross over, because if one wanted to enter into or leave Bajina Basta, one had to go through a police checkpoint. Whoever wanted to join the war in Skelani, to defend the Serb people there, had to report to those people there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question, however, was the following: Did you know that the units of the Uzice Corps were there prior to the attack on Skelani, what you call the attack on Skelani, that the 16th of January; that they had entered Skelani before that?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may this document please be assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This document is being tendered and received and marked as Defence Exhibit D183.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's move.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance, please. I would like to show the witness document 01857913. It's a document of the Srebrenica municipality War Presidency, dated the 17th of January, 1993. It's a protest sent to the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This document will hopefully shed light on the previous document along the line suggested by my learned colleague, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you please have a look at this document. I will quote the relevant section. This is in relation to a protest sent by the Srebrenica municipality War Presidency to the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Paragraph 2, the third and fourth paragraphs, the beginning of the fourth paragraph: "The artillery attacks have been intensified since January 1st this year, and the former Yugoslav army aviation carries out bombardment of the Srebrenica region every day, and aircraft take off from the airport of Ponica [phoen] near Uzice. The world public knows very little about this. In the night between January 15th and 16th this year, the Uzice Corps crossed the bridge in Skelani, and from Bajina Basta, crossed with 12 tanks, seven armed personnel carriers, and a number of trucks, and carried out an attack on the territory of the defenders. From that moment, fierce fighting has been going on, and they -- and it is still going on as we are sending this report. In the above-mentioned fighting, the aggressor even uses their aviation, and as a result, over 100 civilians have been killed. The advance of the aggressor has been stopped, but fresh forces are being drawn from Serbia and introduced into Basil," and so on and so forth. Mr. Gligic, is it not true that the attacks against the remaining Muslim settlements of the Srebrenica enclave, including Srebrenica itself, started to mount, from the direction of Skelani, from the beginning of January 1993?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Do you want to give this document a number?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will be D184. Now let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you, Mr. Gligic, if it was true that the attacks against the remaining Muslim settlements of the Srebrenica enclave, including Srebrenica itself, intensified from the direction of Skelani, from early January 1993 on.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it not true that there was intense shelling from the areas of Jezero and Bajina Basta in the direction of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had to notice a presence of tanks and APCs in Skelani during the first half of January 1993.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will now move on to what happened on the 16th of January, 1993, or rather, the attack. My question is: What happened on the 16th of January was an attempt by the Muslim forces to foil horrible attacks against the civilian population of Srebrenica from the direction of Skelani, midway through January 1993, was it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your testimony, you described the attackers on the 16th of January, 1993, and how they were firing at everything that moved across the bridge to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is true, in fact, isn't it, that at the time, as well as in previous days, forces were being infiltrated from Serbia across that bridge with tanks and APCs and soldiers?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described that the attackers were firing towards your house and the police station; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The whole of Skelani was attacked, the entire town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that near the police station is where the command post of the Skelani Battalion was positioned?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of the command post. But the command itself, the headquarters, was at Jezero.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you do agree that part of the command was there, after all.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is also true, isn't it, that the police station itself was a stronghold with many armed men in it, and that they were, in fact, returning fire when the attack came? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that no one was firing at the attackers from the police station?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember clearly the day of the attack at Skelani. I'll never forget it. At the time, the only people left in Skelani were women, children, and small babies.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we please caution the witness to answer my questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any firing from the police station? Was anyone firing at the attackers from the police station?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You personally, your brother, and a great number of other fighters were, in fact, returning fire and firing on the attackers from your positions at the time.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Actually, there was shooting on all sides. There was crossfire being exchanged, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The forces from Serbia joined the fighting very soon, and the Muslims were quickly repelled; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The attack started at 5.30, and firing by the Muslim forces stopped at about 1100 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did say that, at one point in time, the shooting stopped and you saw the attackers looting, did you not?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Above our houses, in Skelani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among them, there were plenty of civilians, women and children; that's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not women and not children. Women and civilians taking things, mounting things on cattle and then driving their cattle on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You told us yesterday that 57 persons were killed in Skelani during the attack.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not persons. Women, children, and civilians, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown his own statement, dated 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's clear this, because there seems to be a question. The question was: You told us yesterday that 57 persons were killed in Skelani during the attack, and then somehow the transcript that we have is: "No, not persons. Women, children, and civilians, that's what I said." But women are civilians and children are civilians, no? So can you clear this up for us? Why not persons? Because women are persons just the same. Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, what I'm saying is they are human beings. Maybe I did not express myself very clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It could be. If you didn't, could you please express yourself better now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'm telling you, on that day, human beings were killed, women, children, and men, all of them human beings. All of them were killed during the attack against Skelani.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But were they civilians or not civilians? Or were they mixed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. For the most part, what I'm trying to say is that 90 per cent or higher, women and children, handicapped people who were not fit for military service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you please look at your own statement from the year 2000, on page 12, and then continue on page 13 of the B/C/S. In the English, it's all on page 12. You state that, on the 17th of January, 1992, you helped to identify 30 bodies. Could you please look at that part of your statement. Please have a look at the list you provided. You said you helped identify these persons. Did you know these persons personally?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ivanka Popovic, Branko Jakovljevic, Dimitrijevic --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, no, these are not the persons I mean. If you could look at the very beginning, Milorad Rakic, the first list on that page.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milorad Rakic is from Cosici. Damjan Maksimovic and Zeljko Pavlovic, Vidosava Trifunovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. The question was a simple one. We don't need to go through the list one by one. Look at it, please. This should be, according to what it says here, a list that you gave to the Office of the Prosecution. You're being asked to look at it and to confirm to us that you knew these persons, these 20 individuals, personally. Just answer yes or no. If you didn't, it doesn't matter. It's not going to change much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So your next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew their year of birth?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know when they were born, but I know these people. We lived together. I can't know personal information in relation to each and every one of these individuals, when they were born.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were the one who provided this information to the OTP; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I was questioning in Skelani for about ten days, and this is the sort of information that you can go to Kapela for. Even now you can go to the morgue, go to the cemetery, where the people were buried, and take this information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you knew Milorad Rakic.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew Milena Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's already said that he knew them all, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm putting it to you that Milorad Rakic, Milena Stevanovic, Radosava Rakic, that none of the persons bearing these names lived in the territory of the municipality of Srebrenica, Bratunac, or the territory of Skelani, in 1991.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where they lived or where they live. I know that these people got killed in Skelani, and I know the villages they hail from, for all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am submitting an excerpt from the census of Bosnia and Herzegovina from April 1991 for the municipalities of Bratunac, Han Pijesak, Rogatica, Srebrenica, and Zepa, and the excerpt is accompanied by an official letter from the Federal Institute of Statistics. And there the names and surnames of all the Stevanovics and Rakics is contained. Milorad Rakic, Radosava Rakic, and Milena Stevanovic did not exist in the territories of the municipalities of Srebrenica and Bratunac in 1991. Could these excerpts please be assigned an exhibit number, and then I will ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. These are being given -- this document is being given exhibit number -- Defence Exhibit D184. Could you take us straight to the pages? They are not numbered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This will be D185, sorry. My apologies to you. All right. In any case, you've made the submission. This will be D185, and we'll find it. Yes, let's move.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moreover, Mr. Gligic, none of these persons is entered into the registry of debts.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can I have the usher's assistance to place a letter from the municipality of Srebrenica on the ELMO from a general administration office in Skelani, January 17th, 2005. The letter is signed by the notary, and enclosed is my request to the Ministry of Security to deliver the names of several persons from Skelani. Could we please take a look at the letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, before learned counsel proceeds, the document we've now identified as D185, I don't believe that she's asked the witness a question about it. I believe she herself --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, and I would have stopped her if she had asked him a question on it, because --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And I also just want to state that I think Mr. Gligic's testimony was that he didn't know where they were in 1991, but that he knew the villages they originally came from. So I don't know whether we're going to clarify that with a question in relationship to this document, or the relevance that the document now has to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's enough -- enough for us. Yes. Now, this document, this is being given D186. Yes, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at the letter. Under item 1, there reads "Milorad Rakic," and the municipality says that in the Skelani registry records, there are no data concerning his death. Milena Stevanovic, under item 6, rather, Milena Stevanovic, under item 2, and Radisava Rakic, under item 6, no data in the register of debts in Skelani. I will move on to a different matter now. Are you quite sure, sir, that Milorad Rakic was killed on that day in Skelani?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When talking about names, I can tell you that there's nobody in the world who could memorise all these names. I know that there were people from Cosici, from Skelani. So I knew these people. Now, where they lived, where they were registered, I'm not going into these matters, nor am I aware of them. It reads here: "Todorovic Gordana." She was born in Skelani and married in Srebrenica. And she moved to Skelani, and then got killed in Skelani.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't need all these details.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My questions will be specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just to make one thing clear. You were not asked to identify these bodies in Skelani, you were asked to identify these bodies in Bajina Basta, no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How shall I put this? Most of the people living in Skelani have dual citizenship, like, for instance, myself --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please answer the question. When you saw these dead bodies, did you see them in Skelani, when you were asked to identify them, or did you see them in the morgue in Bajina Basta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We transported all the corpses to the Bajina Basta morgue, because we did not have a morgue in Skelani. And the people who were authorised to register these bodies, they did so in Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We are there. Let's move.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, you knew Rosa Nedic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was her name again?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Rosa Nedic. Her name is on the list.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nedzic? That's the Grizevici [phoen] village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew when she was born, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm putting it to you, Mr. Gligic, that you provided incorrect information in relation to these persons. I'm putting it to you that Rakic Milorad died at least 20 days -- 20 years before the start of the war. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His youngest child was born in 1936.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could this letter be assigned an exhibit number, unless it already has one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I just ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know why we gave it a number already, but it will be D186, in any case. D186.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the witness to look at the name Blagomir Mitrovic, who was born in 1943 -- Blagomir Nikolic, born in 1943.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you quite sure, Mr. Gligic, that this person got killed in Skelani, and that he was among the dead, be it in Srebrenica, be it in Bajina Basta?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you mean? What do you mean, you don't know? If you're stating to the Office of the Prosecutor in your statement that, on the 17th of January, in the medical centre in Bajina Basta, you saw a body and you identified him as being -- belonging to that of Blagomir Nikolic, how come you come here now and tell us that you don't know? You either recognised -- you either recognised that body or you didn't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The bodies that we transported to the morgue, I did not witness their deaths. I only know that I took them over there. And these lists were drawn up on the basis of the data provided at the health centre, or rather, at the morgue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But you stated to the Office of the Prosecutor, and you also stated earlier on today, that the list of 20 persons that you see here on page 12 of your statement, or whichever page it is in your own language, you identified as dead bodies on that occasion, and that you knew them all personally. So I can't understand how you could possibly come here and explain to us that -- in one minute, you're stating that you recognise Blagomir Nikolic, the dead body of Blagomir Nikolic, and now you're telling us that you don't know. I mean, you either recognised him or you -- you recognised that dead body or you didn't recognise that body.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time of death of these people, I knew the villages they originated from and I knew their names, and I drove them over to the morgue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question is a very simple one: It's being put to you that perhaps you're wrong when you identified a body belonging to Blagomir Nikolic. But you did state to the Prosecution that, on the 17th of January, you identified a dead body as belonging to Blagomir Nikolic. Did you identify a dead body as belonging to Blagomir Nikolic, or didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you, Your Honour, 12 years have elapsed since. I'm simply saying, and there's evidence to prove that, that I transported these dead bodies. But this is -- this took place a long time ago, and I really wouldn't be able to tell you their names now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but when you made a statement to the Prosecution, you did not hesitate at all in giving a whole list of 20 persons who are dead, another list of 10 persons who were injured, and further, other lists that we have in the statement. Was this list invented by the officer from the Office of the Prosecutor -- investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor, or was it a list that you yourself gave to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the Prosecution asked me to provide information in the process of my interview, I went to the morgue in Bajina Basta and they have records there, dated records, therefore, containing dates when I was transporting dead bodies there. And that was the list that I delivered to the gentleman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That is understandable. But in your statement, you say: "I think it was on the afternoon of the 17th of January, 1992, that I was asked by the police inspector in Skelani to attend the medical centre in Bajina Basta to give a statement about what I saw and did on that day. They also wanted me to help identify the bodies. I went to the morgue and I saw many bodies which had been covered with sheets, apart from their heads. I assisted in identifying about 30 local villagers. They were ..." And then we have a list of 20. Did you identify these 20? Did you see the body, the dead body, of Milorad Rakic? Did you see and identify the dead body of Damjan Maksimovic? Did you see the dead body of Andjelko Pavlovic? Did you see the dead body of Blagomir Nikolic? This is what is being asked of you. Or you saw a number of dead bodies, you didn't care who they were, but when you were asked by the Prosecution, you told them, Look at the list, those were the bodies. Which is the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The gentleman who asked me to go and find the information out, at the time, Mr. Ostoje was an inspector at the SUP, and since he lived in Srebrenica but hailed from Sekovici and worked in the SUP in Srebrenica, I was telling that person who the individual persons were, where they hailed from, from Skelani and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that doesn't answer the question. My question is a very simple one, and you have been trying to avoid answering it for the past 15 minutes. You told the Prosecution, the officer of the Prosecution, I went to Bajina Basta, and there I saw a lot of bodies, and I helped in identifying a number of those bodies; I'm going to give you the list; these are the persons I identified in Bajina Basta. Did you identify those dead bodies, or did you just give a list and never really identified any of those dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ostoje would ask me who the individual corpses were, and I would tell them their names and where the villages hailed from. This refers solely to the people that I transported over to Bajina Basta, and I provided him the names of the people. Whether I was wrong in some of the names, but I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you're telling us that the records that exist in Bajina Basta, referring to the dead bodies that were transported on that day by yourself, indicate names that you yourself gave to the persons over there? Am I right or am I wrong? In other words, if the records in Bajina Basta say that the body of Andja Janjic and the body of Dragomir Nikolic were transported to the morgue in Bajina Basta on the 17th of December, it's because you told the authorities over there that that is the body of Blagomir Nikolic, that is the body of Andja Janjic, that is the body of Milorad Rakic. Am I right or am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you did identify these bodies, these dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So when it's being put to you that Milorad Rakic was -- couldn't have possibly been identified by you because he died 20 years earlier, could you have been wrong? Did you know Milorad Rakic personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew him personally. The man wore this very black coat, and he is very dark complexioned. Not only him, but his entire family.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: A black hat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where was he living before, according to you, before he was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe they have a house in Bajina Basta and in Skelani. I know for sure that they do have a house in Skelani, whereas for Bajina Basta, I'm not sure whether they just had a plot of land or a house as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And before you transported his dead body on the 17th of December, when did you see him last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw the man in the summer and autumn of 1992. He was a farmer. He was -- he had cattle to attend to, and he had his land that he cultivated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance, please. I would like to show the witness D45. D45.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document is a list of soldiers from the Bratunac military post who were killed between 1990 and 1996. If you could please look at the page that bears the number 411. The names are listed and numbered. If you can please look at 411. The name is Blagomir Nikolic, born 1943, in Kalimanici. Blagomir Nikolic, born 1943. Date of death, 24th of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. February, 1993, in Kalimanici. Mr. Gligic, do you agree that you could not possibly have identified this man at the morgue on the 17th of January, 1993, then?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could he have been killed on the 24th when, to begin with, there was no attack on the 24th? All the people who were killed in that period of time were killed on the 16th of January. Later, there was a cease-fire or a truce, peace, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll just move on. I think this is a pointless exercise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've shown you a document claiming that the date of death was the 24th of February, 1993. Can you just please keep the Defence exhibit for a while, D45. We shall be requiring this document for a while longer. Witness, yesterday, you told us that Fakovici and Ratkovici had been torched and looted. I will now ask you questions in relation to this. I need you to just tell us what you personally witnessed and saw in these two places. When were you in Ratkovici, as a matter of fact?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Ratkovici -- well, I can't remember the date. It was summertime, and I think the month was June. Whether early June or -- I think it was in early June, unless I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement to the OTP in 2000, you said that you were there on the 20th of June, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Ratkovici -- well, I can't give you the exact date. I was only there once. I said what I did there, and there's evidence to corroborate my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on what was it that you told the Prosecutor that you were in Ratkovici on the 20th of June, 1992? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the date. I know that once I was there, and that was when Ratkovici was attacked. I came to Fakovici. I remember that we left the car there. And a group of people, together with the locals, set out on foot towards Ratkovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Therefore, you claim that it was only once that you were in Ratkovici, in June 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, only once, when we buried bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you arrived in Ratkovici after the attack; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You arrived, in fact, several hours later.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not see a single attacker there, did you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not see a single person stealing anything from any of the houses.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Ratkovici? No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not see a single person set fire to any of the houses.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrived, the houses were already in ashes but still smoking. Whatever was there had already been torched.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. But please, can you pay closer attention to my question. I'm asking about what you say personally, what you witnessed. You did not see a single person set fire to any of the houses. You personally did not see.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in Ratkovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on what you saw in person, there's no way you can say whether those homes were looted by elderly people, by women, by children; in one word, by civilians?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The strategy --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please answer my question? Based on your personal experience.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Ratkovici, I did not see anyone taking things away or killing people, as for the Muslims there. We only arrived later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That closes the issue. I mean, if he didn't see anyone, he can't explain any further than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, you were asked by the OTP as to your opinion on how buildings in Ratkovici had been torched.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to that, let me ask you: You have no special knowledge that would allow you to conduct an investigation on how exactly the houses were torched, do you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the investigations in our area, people who were in war, who know about war, people who were eyewitnesses know exactly what the human factor amounts to, human force. People were not just committing suicides and massacring their own, if you know what I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, witness, I asked you this: You have no special knowledge that would allow you to conduct an investigation on the causes of the houses being burned down?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean I have no authority?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, it's a very simple question. If you see a house in ashes, still smoking, how can you say how that -- how it came by that that house ended up in ashes? How can you say that it did not catch fire as a result of a short circuit? How can you say that it did not catch fire as a result of arson? How can you say that it did not catch fire in one way or in another? You can only say that you saw it burning, or that you saw it in ashes, still smoking. But you can't say how it all happened. Even if you think that it happened maliciously, you can't say whether it was torched, whether a Zolja was fired into it. You can't say, because you weren't there. You may say with regard to other places, but you can't say with regard to the houses in Ratkovici. You can't even say whether the people, the inhabitants themselves, set the houses on fire. Not that it is likely, but you can't say it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I arrived in Ratkovici, I realised that all the houses had been burned down. The pigs and home animals had been slaughtered. People had been slaughtered. There were bodies lying around. I buried one man with bits of shrubbery. I know his son. His son works in Zvornik now. This is something that I remember with great clarity, and this is something that I'll never be able to forget.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And still you didn't give me one iota of what should have been your answer. Nothing. You have not even tried to answer my question, or else you're trying to avoid answering my question. When you saw those houses in ashes, still smoking, you could only draw one conclusion, that maybe they had been burned, but you don't know how they were set on fire, what caused the burning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's quite correct. But my opinion is, as given in my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But that's your opinion. We're not interested in opinions, we're interested in facts. God forbid that we acquit or convict persons on opinions here. Yes, I think we need to stop for a break. We'll have a 25-minute break, starting from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's conclude this, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, yesterday you said that the victims of the attack on Ratkovici were, for the most part, elderly men and women not wearing uniforms; in other words, they were civilians. Now, that's not true, is it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I said was that they were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please, again, be shown D45, a document that was left with the witness. Can you please turn to page 457 through to 491. Your Honours, I'm not going through all the names of the fighters who were killed in Ratkovici, because this was something that we discussed with previous witnesses. I would like the witness, however, to have a look at some of these names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you please look at 464. The name is Zivan Prodanovic, son of Petar, born on the 16th of January, 1966, in the village of Ratkovici, killed on the 21st of June, 1992, in Ratkovici. Next, if you can please turn the page and look at 495. Milutin Rankic, son of Obrad, born on the 15th of May, 1944, in Ratkovici. Place of death, Ratkovici. Date of death, the 21st of June, 1992. And then if you can, again, turn the page, please, and look at number 549. Nikola Stanovic, son of Todor, born in 1958, in Ratkovici, killed on the 21st of June, 1992. Next, 551, Stanojevic, son of Vladislav, born on the 16th of November, 1949, in Ratkovici, killed on the 21st of June, 1992, in Ratkovici. Mr. Gligic, do you agree that these persons - you can see their respective years of birth - were young, or at least relatively young back in 1992, which is when they were killed? Their names are on the list of soldiers who were members of the Bratunac military post. Therefore, Mr. Gligic, you were not telling the truth when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has not answered as yet.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was in Ratkovici, I don't know exactly how many bodies there were. I only know the ones that I buried. I know the name of that man. I know his last name and I know who his son is. His son worked at the Bratunac SUP, but now he works in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. Can you explain to me where the contradiction lies, Madam Vidovic? Because the question that you put to him earlier on was that yesterday he said that the majority were civilians, which basically means that there was a minority, and you have only mentioned or referred him to four persons. So how does that clash with his testimony? Could you explain, please? He never said that there were no militaries or soldiers or non-civilians who got killed in Ratkovici on the 21st of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at the outset, I stated that there are at least ten persons on this list who were killed on the 21st of June, 1992. I also said that I will not go through the entire list. The witness stated that those killed were mostly elderly men and women, and what I gave him were names of people who were young. But I can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you said that, right after the attack on the 21st of June, you had seen the body of the late Stojan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stojan?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Stojan Stevanovic. You spoke about his sexual organ.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we crossed the village, Ratkovici I mean, the people who were with me said that his last name was Stevanovic. I saw that his organ had been severed from his body and placed in his mouth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, please, the essence of my question concerns this: Did you see Stojan right after the attack on Ratkovici, on the 21st of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrived in the village of Ratkovici, on the way into the village, that's when I saw him. And then the locals there told me his3030 name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm putting it to you that you did not see Stojan Stevanovic at the time. You could not have seen him, the reason being he only died on the 27th of June, 1992, as late as that. That is the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he has a brother who worked in Skelani as a teacher. He worked in Skelani as a teacher, and his brother used to come to Skelani. And this man was brought over and he was buried right there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, again, let us turn our attention to D45, number 557, Stojan Stevanovic, son of Dragomir, born in Ratkovici, killed on the 27th of June, 1992, in Ratkovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, was there fighting in Ratkovici on the 27th of June, 1992? If you know, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But after the 21st of June, 1992, are you aware of any further fighting in Ratkovici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Next question, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will ask you briefly about something in relation to the attacks on Krnici and Malina. You said that a lot of civilians were killed there, including Boban the priest. Can you please, again, look at -- can you please, again, look at D45, the list of Bratunac Brigade soldiers that were killed. Look at the name under 269, Boban Lazarevic, son of Spasoje. It's true, isn't it, Mr. Gligic, that Boban Lazarevic, the priest, relinquished his vows, and before the war he was involved actively in bringing volunteers in from Serbia into the area, and he led the Serbian population of the villages in expelling their Muslim neighbours from the surrounding villages. Is that not a fact?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The truth of the matter is, Boban, the priest, was killed in combat on the 5th of July, 1992, as a soldier and not as a civilian, in Krnici?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if he was wearing his priest robe or civilian clothes. I know that there was a church in that village. He was there. That's where he was killed. We pulled his body out after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You were quite decided yesterday when you said, in relation to Fakovici, that all civilians there were killed; is that true?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have this house, and the owner's last name was Markovic. In that house --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, please answer the question. Just the question. It's a very simple question. You are being asked to confirm, or not to confirm, what you said yesterday; namely, that in relation to Fakovici, according to you, all civilians were killed. Just answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Next question, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm putting it to you that at least 13 soldiers, members of the Bratunac Brigade, got killed on that day in Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How does that change his testimony? Because his testimony, according to you and according to the previous question, was that -- you asked him to confirm that all civilians were killed. This is what I have here on the transcript. You did not ask him to -- about non-civilians and about soldiers, and I don't think he ever testified about soldiers getting killed or not getting killed in Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, he testified yesterday decisively by saying that all those killed in Fakovici were civilians, and he confirmed so today, at least that's how I understood it. And in addition to this, I would like to show the witness a part of his statement given to the investigators on the page 03063356, where he said: "In this attack, 22 persons were killed, all of whom were civilians." And I'm claiming --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead with your question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm putting it to you, Mr. Gligic, that at least 13 of these were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You stated that you had gone to Fakovici on the 6th of October, 1992. You never saw any attackers there either, nor can you state anything in relation to them.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never saw the manner in which the houses were burned down, if any were, either; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will move on to a different matter. Yesterday, you told us that you knew Naser Oric from before the war. Yesterday, you explained that you saw him just before the outbreak of the war, in 1992. However, I will show to you your statement for the investigators in 2000 when you stated that you saw Naser Oric, who was surrounded by a group of armed Muslims, back in early 1991.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the gentleman wearing a police uniform. It was after Herzegovina that he arrived in a Golf vehicle to this cafe named Merima where Ahmo Tihic was seated. At this particular table, there were also members of the reserve police forces, but they were not seated at the same table with him but at a different table.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm asking you simply what the truth is. Is the truth what you told to the investigators back in 2000 when you claimed that you had met Naser Oric in 2001, when he was wearing a beard? Yesterday, you told us quite a different thing, that you met him just before the war; that he wasn't wearing a beard. These are two completely different statements. What is true?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have not been citing the dates as I told them. I told you that it was prior to the war, in the community centre, where the gentleman was working out in the gym, that I saw him in civilian clothes. And I saw him in Bratunac in civilian clothes. And I saw the gentleman wearing a uniform in the Merima cafe, owned by Tihic Behim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm drawing Your Honours' attention to the part of the 2000 statement where he says the following: "The next person I'm going to be talking about is Naser Oric, who gathered a group of armed Muslims around him. I heard that he had become their leader. I got to know Naser Oric in early 1991, in a hall ..." And so on and so forth. So which of these accounts is the true one, Mr. Gligic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Referring to the next statement, Madam Vidovic, the next paragraph says: "The next time I saw Naser Oric was between the 5th and 10th of April, at a Skelani cafe." This is the Merima cafe.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. Yes, that's correct. But I was referring to that part of the witness' statement when he was telling about him meeting Naser Oric and getting to know him for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, let's move.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that on the 4th of April, 1992, when you saw Naser Oric, that he was an idol for the Muslims, he was their commander. Do you really maintain that in April 1992, Naser Oric was considered an idol by all the Muslims or a commander of theirs?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The gentleman you're referring to had at the time, at the Srebrenica MUP, a very high position. That was a very influential one. I remember it was Bajram, I cannot forget this, and he was seated at a cafe with the chief of police, who was appointed to his post through political connections. I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, my question was a very specific one. Do you really maintain that he was considered an idol at the time?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or a commander?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An idol, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm putting it to you that at the time he was widely known as a -- one of the bodyguards for the Serbian president, Slobodan Milosevic, and you must know about this.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you're mixing up the dates. This was later on, and what you're talking about was earlier on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When talking about the attacks, you were very certain in assessing yesterday that Naser Oric was the commander of the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I asked you whether Radovan Karadzic, together with the SDS leadership, was stationed at Pale, you answered: "I am not aware of this." This is page 72, line 15. And you added: "I heard this from the media, but I myself don't know anything about it. I was driving an ambulance." And I will put a question to you in relation to this. Mr. Gligic, it seems to me that you know much more about the organisation of the Muslim army than about the basic facts of the Serbian leadership and where it was stationed.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. I know very well that the leadership of Republika Srpska was stationed at Pale, but that's not how you phrased your question. As far as I remember, you asked me whether the War Presidency of Skelani had any contacts with the authorities at the time, and I don't know that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, you claimed that you were merely driving an ambulance; therefore, you never personally attended any meetings of the soldiers of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or any of its commanders.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. But at the beginning of the war, when we were at the cafe, they were having a conversation. I don't know what they were talking about. But when you have a mono-ethnic group gathering, then you can imagine what they're talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, please listen closely to my questions. My question was: You yourself never personally attended any meetings held by the Muslim commanders.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's why I'm putting it to you again that this part of your testimony concerning the Muslim commanders attacking Skelani is based on assumptions, surmises, rumours.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You yourself didn't have any reliable information in regard to this.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, in Skelani and around Skelani, the entire municipality, including the Muslims and the Serbs, almost all of them knew who the commander in Srebrenica was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you yourself had no reliable information, other than what you heard talked around.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people, and I mean the Muslims, be it civilians or soldiers, who were captured during these combat activities and were then exchanged, from these Muslims I found out that Naser was the commander for Srebrenica. And there were a great many footages that I watched in Skelani, in Bratunac, where I watched his speeches and his actions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of the fact that you were a police officer conducting investigations about the Muslims, allowing you to make such conclusions.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a police officer, but I am a resident of Skelani. And any resident of a town, whichever town it be, is interested in knowing who the commander of the police is, who a manager of a public company is. That's only natural.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, you must be aware of the fact that many Muslims who were questioned in Skelani were subjected to all manner of torture.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, nor do I know that there were any interrogations. I was unable to find out anything about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I will move on to a different question. Yesterday, you told us about Ahmo Tihic and that he was trafficking in arms; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You yourself never bought any weapons from him, did you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself did not. But the people I socialised with and I lived with can tell you his name. He was born in 1961. Zurijet Leskovica was telling us about this. And I claim to you for a fact that I knew that Ahmo Tihic was arming all the weapons in Skelani, and that he was demanding high sums of money in exchange for these weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I'll move on to a different question. In June 2000, you told the investigators that you took part in an exchange that occurred on the 29th of January, 1993. A moment ago, I showed you -- I showed you the statement --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dates that I provided. Now, whether I would be able to tell you the exact dates today, 12 years later, I don't know. But there are eyewitnesses, Muslims, who were being exchanged and who know that I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are quite certain, Mr. Gligic, that you yourself took part in the exchange of the persons, Milena Mitrovic, Branko Mitrovic, Sane Mitrovic, and so on. Are you quite sure about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. And Mr. Ramiz, who was a representative on their side, and Mr. Mandza from whom we were taking papers when we would show up and surrender our papers to them. These papers served the purpose of them agreeing on their future cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Do you have a re-examination, Ms. Sellers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will have to have a re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I believe it's going to be at least 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I meant to finish with this witness today. This is misleading -- misleading the Trial Chamber completely, and creating a situation where we cannot plan. So you have five minutes more, and you have to conclude, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, did you have any contacts with Ivan Ivanovic -- with Ilija Ivanovic, after his exchange?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was on the 26th of February that Ilija Ivanovic was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you talk to him about his captivity, his detention?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at that particular point in time, no. I brought the gentleman over to Skelani, and I believe he was taken by car from there to the health centre to be examined. Later on - some time elapsed before he recovered - I would see him occasionally, and I still see him occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we turn into private session briefly, because I have to name a witness, and it's a very important matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, Mr. Gligic, do you really believe that the people we saw on the video, whose houses had been torched and looted, and who had to live under such difficult conditions out in the woods, really needed ordering to burn the homes of those who had done this to them?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand both the Serbian and the Muslim people, but not everyone is like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, this fact about Oric giving orders to those people is not something that you mentioned in your detailed statement to the investigators, an 18-page statement, in fact. Can you just answer my question briefly?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I forgot that, but there are things that I'm remembering even now. It has been 12 years since, madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You concluded your testimony yesterday by saying that, in the Podrinje area, both Serbs and Muslims committed atrocities, but that Muslims had the upper hand in this. Is it possible, Mr. Gligic, for you to ignore the genocide that occurred in this area in 1995 to such a terrifying extent?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you didn't understand. I'm talking about the Skelani area. Whoever committed crimes must be held to account. The people at large can't be blamed for anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it is true that it was precisely the people from Skelani, the Skelani Battalion, who murdered a lot of these people, including Ahmo Tihic, who you testified about yesterday, is it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really have no idea where Ahmo Tihic was killed. I don't have any information on that. I don't know. I know when he came to Skelani with his father, I shook hands with him, and his father, a man called Mujo, told me that his son --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why are you giving us this extra information? No one asked you for it. You have absolutely disrupted our schedule, our time schedule, by going on and on and on, and giving information that was not asked from you. Are you finished, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll try to be as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you could finish in less than ten minutes, please. And concentrate on what is relevant to the case, because I am very much afraid that we are missing completely the trees for the wood or the wood for the trees. Re-examined by Ms. Sellers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, you testified earlier, and Ms. Vidovic made reference to your statement, about the fact that you saw Naser Oric in a gym in 1991. At that time period, did you meet him in the sense that you had a conversation with him and you were introduced to him properly?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you say that you knew him, you met him, that means that you knew him when you saw him, you knew of him, but that you were not someone who personally spoke with him; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never personally spoke to him, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'd like to have Defence Exhibit 179.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, I think you've been asked questions about that, particularly as to the different units that were stationed in the area. Is it still your testimony that none of these units were stationed within the village of Skelani in July 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is still my position that none of the mentioned units were, with the exception of volunteers, from Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gligic, if you would look at the Defence Exhibit -- I'm sorry, I don't have the number for it. It's the one with the ERN number 01857913. Mr. Gligic, is it still your testimony that, during the attack in Skelani, that there were no APCs, tanks, or trucks, or any presence, to your knowledge, of the Uzice Corps?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no corps there and no tanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I would like to go to Defence Exhibit 178, which is a Human Rights Watch report. We don't necessarily have to give it to the defendant -- to the witness. I will read it out loud. Madam Vidovic read a section of this Human Rights Watch report. There is one sentence that came after she finished a paragraph, and I will read it to you now. In reference to Bosnian Muslims going to Bajina Basta, it says: "Others were driven from Bajina Basta to Loznica (in Serbia) in six buses and two trucks. In Loznica, the refugees were taken back to the Bosnian town of Kalesija." Does it remain your testimony that many Bosnian Muslims went from Skelani to Bajina Basta and then possibly to further places in Serbia? And, I'm sorry, let me situate this. This would be in April or May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you said about the time frame was quite accurate, the months you mentioned. It is still my position today that the Muslims went to the Red Cross at Bajina Basta and they -- they went on, travelled on to other towns in Serbia, wherever they were received. Some went to Macedonia, some to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Lastly, I would like to ask you, Mr. Gligic, is it still your testimony that refugees came into Skelani, and that there were both Bosnian Serb refugees and Bosnian Muslim refugees that were in the area of Skelani during the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period of time, there were Muslims, right, those who had left, and you had people coming to Skelani, Serbs from Tuzla, from whatever Bosnian towns they were in at the time, whichever Bosnian towns were in today's federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to show the Defence video, just a 30-second portion of that. I believe -- is it up on everyone's Sanction?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not yet. It is now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, I would like to read to you what is said underneath, just for purposes of it not being translated into your language. It appears that a person is saying: "We were first down there on Ravnica without cottages, without anything. We were receiving refugees that came from all sides." Is this consistent with the testimony that you've given the Trial Chamber that refugees from all sides were in and around the Skelani area during this time period?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can we clarify whether "sides" means geographical or ethnicity? Otherwise it's confusing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think it's confusing at all, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: "All sides" could easily mean east, west, north, south.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "We were receiving refugees that came from all sides."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's probably what it does mean, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's self-explanatory.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'll just repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this consistent with the testimony that you've given, Mr. Gligic? That in the Skelani area, there were refugees that were both Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Serb? You can just answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question. Can you please repeat the question. What exactly do you want to know?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly. I'd like to know that when you see this image here, and then where it is saying, and I'm translating it for you, in essence, "we were receiving refugees that came from all sides," is that assistant with your testimony that you gave to the Trial Chamber that, in the Skelani area, in 1992, from the spring throughout, that there were refugees that were Bosnian Serb refugees and Bosnian Muslim refugees, that were in the area?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hate to object, it's just as if my learned friend is trying to get misleading evidence from this witness. If he were just to be asked, Do you think that Bosnian Serb refugees were being accepted by the Bosnian Muslim refugees whom we see in the video, then we can get a clear answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But he said he was not understanding the question, so what do you expect? It's a simple question. Whether what this gentleman is saying coincides with what he believes to be the truth or whether it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's why the witness is so confused, because is it consistent in what sense? He's being invited to say yes, it's consistent, and then my learned friend will get to what she wants to get. But, in fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, when I tell you that someone says, "we were receiving refugees that came from all sides," what do you understand? This gentleman here, with his hand on the tree, resting, is saying "we were receiving refugees that came from all sides." What is he telling us? What kind of refugees? What does he mean, refugees that came from all sides?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand the question now. This frame shows that, and the gentleman said that too. They were only receiving Muslim refugees from some of the villages. I'm not sure if that was the case or not. I can neither confirm or deny.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is making the confusion more confounded. This is making confusion more confounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Through no fault of mine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm certainly not blaming you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour looked at me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I honestly think that I -- I honestly don't think I should burden the interpreters, the rest of the staff, any further. I think I'm going to ask my colleagues to agree to stop here. Mr. Gligic, you need to return again tomorrow, and blame yourself for it. We are adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 2nd day of February, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
